reason: Bicoloured perianth is normal. The French examples (bicolore, coloration variée) fit.
Flexuous involucral bracts or bract tips are a real phyllary character, and flexuous reads as sinuous. One example is about the tips, but the bearer is the same.
Wrong reading. 'Bristlelike spines' describes the shape of a spine, which resembles a bristle. The thorn is not covered in bristles. Bristlelike should be a shape, not the hairy-surface term.
A calyx or its limb can flare outward. The examples are correct.
The margins of a corolla lip can be involute. Strictly, the margin is the bearer, but the lip carries it.
Tepals can be present or absent, for example in distal or unisexual flowers. The examples fit.
'Bent forward' fits bent. 'Angled' (one side angled) is an angular shape or a fold, not a bend. A rule would need to map 'angled' to a different term and keep 'bent' or 'curved' here.
Spikes can be elliptic in outline. The ellipsoid examples are close in meaning.
Spoon-shaped petals are common (spatulate or cochleariform). The examples are correct.

Wrong reading. 'Valvate' is how the valves meet, and 'solitary or paired' is a count or arrangement of capsules. Neither is a spatial pattern of the capsule itself. Handle them with a count rule or an aestivation term.
A leaf base has a measurable width. The examples are measurements.
A perianth bristle (as in Cyperaceae) can be slender. The examples fit.
Bristle length is a standard character, given as a size or as a ratio to the achene.
A petal apex can be notched or emarginate. 'Apical notch 1-3 mm' is a size of the notch, which is close enough.
Bud scales can be densely silky-hairy (sericeous). The examples are correct.
Floral corona parts (lobes, spurs, scales) are described as oblong. One example, 'horned oblong spur', is a spur of the corona, which is acceptable.
Scale leaves can have an acuminate apex. The English and French examples fit.
Wrong reading. 'Septate' (cross-walls in the leaf) is not 'split'. The PATO term means divided or broken, and 'not splitting when pressed' is an unrelated test. Septation needs its own term.
Stamens can be suberect or erect-spreading. Some examples (connectives, spur) are other parts, but the pair is fine.

Wrong reading. 'Radiant' flowers (Apiaceae, Asteraceae) have enlarged outer petals or ray florets. 'Radial presentation' is symmetry. Neither means radiating in the PATO sense. It needs a rule for 'radiant' (the outer flowers are enlarged) and a symmetry term.
Labellum lobes and their divisions can be filiform. The examples fit.
Leaf teeth can have a hair-fringed (ciliate) margin. The examples fit.
Hyaline means translucent, and peristome teeth in mosses can have hyaline margins or tips. Hyaline is a good fit for transparent.

'Capillary branches' describes the branches or axes of the inflorescence (hair-thin), not the inflorescence itself. A rule would need to send the quality to the branch or axis part and decide whether capillary maps to fibrillary or to a thin or filiform term.
A flower can be pedicellate (it has a pedicel). The French examples are about the pedicel's length and attachment, not whether it is present, but the pair is meaningful.
Sporophylls (as in Selaginella) can have a dentate or denticulate margin. The examples fit, even though one mentions a keel.
Sporophylls have a colour, for example green or yellow.
A staminode can have an entire margin or lobe. The examples fit.
The carpophore (a fruit column in Apiaceae and Caryophyllaceae) can be present or absent. Carpophore is treated as the columella here, which is acceptable.
Achenes are commonly laterally compressed, and the negated examples are fine too.
Cymes can be pedunculate (stalked). The examples are correct.
Resin canals are counted (2, 3-9). Counts use the amount attribute.
The gynostemium (orchid column) can be hairy. The examples describe the hairs.
A leaf sheath, or its apex, can be narrow. Some examples are about the apex, but the pair is fine.
Auricles of grass leaf sheaths are often deciduous. The examples fit.
Vittae (oil tubes) can be small or minute. The examples fit.
Pinnules (the ultimate divisions of a fern frond) have a colour, for example green.
Pinnules can be oblique in orientation. 'Oblique at base' is about the base shape, but the pair is meaningful.
Calyx lobes can be thickened, as at the apex. The examples are close enough.
The orchid labellum, its epichile and its lobes can be triangular. The French examples fit.
The perianth tube can be short. The examples fit.
Leaf lobes can be decurrent. 'Base decurrent' is about the base, but the pair is meaningful.

A spathe can be funnel-shaped, but the examples read 'tube funnelform', which is probably a perianth or corolla tube wrongly given the spathe as its bearer. A rule would need to check that the tube belongs to the spathe, not to a flower.
A floral disc can be conspicuous or obvious. The examples fit.
Pappus bristles are capillary (hair-fine), and fibrillary is the closest PATO term. The examples are all about the pappus.
False veins can be present or absent. The English and French examples fit.
Corona lobes can be triangular. The examples fit.
The indusium (fern sorus cover) can be semicircular. The examples fit.
Stems can be nodose (knobbly, with swollen nodes). The French examples fit.
A grass ligule can be fringed with hairs or cilia. The examples fit.
A pedicel can be rough. The examples fit.
Pseudobulbs are often ellipsoid, which is a prolate shape. If PATO has an ellipsoid term that is better, a rule should prefer it. The pair is meaningful.
Plant cells, such as moss alar cells, can be inflated. The examples fit.
A leaf blade, or its margins, can be inrolled. Introverted is an acceptable match.
A cupule wall has a thickness, given in mm. The examples are measurements of that wall.
The epichile (the distal part of the orchid labellum) can be oblong. The examples fit.
An endocarp can be sculptured. The examples fit.

'Lip simple' means an undivided or unlobed lip, which is meaningful. But 'simple hairs' is a hair type, not a shape of the lip. A rule would need to apply 'simple' only when it describes the lip itself and send hair types to the hair.
A hypanthium or floral tube has a width, and 'wide at the throat' is a measurement of it. The pair is meaningful.

A pseudobulb can be grooved (sulcate) or wrinkled, which is a surface character. But 'with chestnut membranous sheaths at base' is a different part. A rule would need to keep surface words (sulcate, grooved, wrinkled) and send sheaths to their own part.
